overview: The TTP223 is about as simple as digital input gets: a tiny breakout with a round copper touch pad on top, wired to a chip that senses the small capacitance change when a finger gets close and flips a digital output pin HIGH or LOW. There's no analog reading and no calibration code required — the chip self-calibrates its baseline on power-up. The one real wrinkle is that many boards carry a solder jumper that switches the output between momentary mode (HIGH only while touched) and toggle/latching mode (each touch flips the output state and holds it) — code written assuming one mode will misbehave in a confusing way on a board set to the other.
simpleSummary: A tiny touch-sensitive pad that outputs a simple HIGH or LOW signal when you touch it, no analog reading needed.

specifications.outputModes: Momentary (HIGH only while touched) or toggle/latching (each touch flips state) — selected by a solder jumper on the board
specifications.responseTime: ~220-260 ms, including a brief self-calibration right after power-up
specifications.standbyCurrent: ~3-6 microamps typical — low enough for battery-powered wake circuits
specifications.detectionRange: A few millimeters through non-metallic material (plastic, glass, thin wood) placed over the pad
specifications.padSize: ~8-10mm diameter round copper pad on typical breakout boards

pinMap.name: VCC
pinMap.function: Power input for the touch sensor IC.
pinMap.currentLimit: ~3-6 microamps standby, low mA during active sensing
pinMap.gotcha: The chip runs a brief self-calibration for roughly a quarter second right after power-up — touching the pad during that window can get baked in as the new 'untouched' baseline, making the sensor seem stuck or unresponsive afterward.

pinMap.name: GND
pinMap.function: Ground reference, shared with the controlling microcontroller.

pinMap.name: OUT
pinMap.function: Digital output that goes HIGH when the pad is touched — behavior depends on the board's solder-jumper mode.
pinMap.currentLimit: ~a few mA, enough to drive an LED directly but not a relay coil
pinMap.gotcha: Whether this pin behaves as a momentary press or a toggling latch is set by a solder jumper on the board, not by your code — code written assuming one mode will silently misbehave on a board jumpered to the other. Check the jumper before debugging your sketch.

useCases.title: Touch button replacement
useCases.scenario: Swap out a mechanical tactile switch for a sealed, no-moving-parts touch pad on a project enclosure.

useCases.title: DIY touch on/off toggle

useCases.title: Wake-from-sleep touch pad

useCases.title: Hidden touch trigger behind an enclosure panel

useCases.title: Simple touch-based game input

oftenConfusedWith: Mechanical tactile push button (physical actuation vs capacitive field sensing, no moving parts)
IR proximity sensor (detects nearby objects through open air vs contact/near-contact sensing through a surface)
oftenUpgradedTo: MPR121 multi-channel capacitive touch IC for several independent touch pads on one board

beginnerMistakes: Assuming momentary mode when the board is actually jumpered to toggle mode, or vice versa, and blaming the code for the mismatch.
Touching the pad during the brief self-calibration window right after power-up, which can bake a false baseline in.
Mounting the pad behind or near metal, which blocks or badly distorts capacitive sensing.
Running a long unshielded wire out to a remote pad, which picks up enough noise to cause false triggers.
Expecting an analog 'how hard/how close' reading — the output is purely digital HIGH/LOW with no proximity gradient.
